title: Onboarding Is All About Relationships
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Writing as both a new hire and a learning and development director, Muth Martinez argues that most hiring managers treat onboarding as a logistics problem when it is really a relational one. Beneath the accounts and introductions, every new hire is asking whether they belong, whether they will be seen and whether it is safe to be honest. She proposes five design questions to ask before building a 30-60-90 plan, covering what the person needs, what belonging looks like, how fast they are expected to get it, what makes safe questioning possible and what would make the process easier. Her plane-versus-rocket image frames the plan as a controlled climb: understanding in the first month, curious contributing in the second and collaborative calibrating in the third. The practical lesson is that managers should resist urgency and keep checking in after the first 60 days.
points: Onboarding that is built around content and access fails because the new hire's real question is whether they belong.
Managers' internal timelines for when someone should get it are usually arbitrary and faster than the year or more that ramp-up often takes.
Designing for psychological safety from day one stops new hires from performing competence instead of asking real questions.
A 30-60-90 plan works as a gradual climb: understand first, contribute with curiosity second, then calibrate collaboratively.
Managers most often pull back in days 61-90, exactly when a genuine check-in about growth signals continued investment.
quotes: The gap between stated values and lived experience doesn’t start at the six-month mark, but on day one. And the reason, I often find, is because most hiring managers view onboarding as a logistics problem, when it’s actually a relational one.
Underneath the entire onboarding experience, a new hire is trying to answer a single question from the moment they walk in the door: do I belong here?

This, ultimately, is what onboarding is actually for. It’s far less about information transfer than it is about trust-building between humans, and understanding this matters enormously for how you design the experience.

Most managers have a rough internal timeline for new hires. It’s usually faster than they’d admit out loud, and almost always shaped by their own experience coming into the role. But that timeline is arbitrary.

The focus here is understanding, not contribution. Your new hire should be in observation mode, meeting people, asking questions, and mapping the landscape. The instinct many new hires experience to demonstrate value early is real but often counterproductive. The most useful thing someone can do in the first month is develop an accurate picture of what they’ve walked into before they try to change any of it, and your job as the manager is to protect that space.

I like to think of it like a plane taking off rather than a rocket launch. A rocket goes from zero to orbit in about 8 minutes, whereas a plane takes off with controlled acceleration followed by a deliberate climb, gaining altitude gradually and steadily until it reaches cruising speed. Both get airborne, but only one is designed to carry everyday people.

This is the phase where managers most often pull back, assuming the new hire has found their footing and is ready to go. Sometimes they have, but more often I find this not to be the case. Don’t take perceived stability for granted.
